beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson four. Water splits, a little, and that changes everything. [[sour]]Lemon juice is sour. [[slip]]Soap feels slippery. [[cell]]Both differ from plain water by tiny amounts of two ions, and a living cell can tolerate very little of either. Let's see where those ions come from, and how we measure them.
beats.split: Zoom into pure water. [[pair]]Two molecules sit joined by a hydrogen bond. [[hop]]Now and then, the hydrogen in that bond crosses over as a bare proton. Its electron stays behind. [[hydronium]]The molecule that gained the proton is a hydronium ion, {{H3O+|H three O plus}}. [[hydroxide]]The one that lost it is a hydroxide ion, {{OH−|O H minus}}. [[short]]For short, we write this as water splitting into {{H+|H plus}} and hydroxide, with H plus understood as a proton riding on a water molecule.
beats.pure: [[rare]]How often does this happen? Rarely. Only about one water molecule in half a billion is split at any moment. [[equal]]Each split makes one H plus and one hydroxide, so in pure water their amounts are equal. [[conc]]We give amounts as concentration, moles per liter, with square brackets around the ion. [[val]]At twenty-five degrees Celsius, both are ten to the minus seven molar. [[kw]]Multiply them and you get ten to the minus fourteen, called K w. In any water solution at this temperature, that product stays the same.
beats.acidbase: Now add a solute. [[acid]]An acid is a proton donor. Hydrochloric acid hands its proton to water, so the H plus concentration rises. [[seesaw]]The product must stay ten to the minus fourteen, so hydroxide falls. [[base]]A base is a proton acceptor. Ammonia pulls a proton off a water molecule, so H plus falls and hydroxide rises. [[same]]Two wordings, one idea: acids raise H plus, and bases lower it.
beats.q1: Quick check. Add a base to pure water.
beats.ph: Those concentrations are tiny and awkward. [[def]]So we use pH, the negative logarithm of the H plus concentration. [[seven]]In pure water, H plus is ten to the minus seven, the log is minus seven, and the pH is seven. [[four]]If H plus is ten to the minus four, the pH is four. [[back]]It also runs backwards: H plus is ten to the minus pH. A pH of eight and a half means three point two times ten to the minus nine molar. [[down]]Notice the direction. More H plus means a lower pH.
beats.scale: [[bar]]The scale runs from zero to fourteen. [[neutral]]Seven is neutral, where H plus equals hydroxide. [[acidic]]Below seven, H plus is greater, and the solution is acidic. [[basic]]Above seven, hydroxide is greater, and the solution is basic. [[ten]]Each step is a factor of ten. [[hund]]So pH three has a hundred times more H plus than pH five: ten times ten.
beats.ex: Where do familiar things sit? [[lemon]]Lemon juice is about pH two. [[coffee]]Black coffee, about five. [[water]]Pure water, seven. [[blood]]Human blood, about seven point four. [[sea]]Seawater, about eight. [[ammonia]]Household ammonia, twelve. [[bleach]]And bleach, thirteen. [[bio]]Most biological fluids fall between six and eight.
beats.q2: Quick check. How many times more acidic?
beats.cells: Why does this matter? [[prot]]A protein is a folded chain, held in shape partly by electric charges along it. [[flood]]Flood the cell with extra H plus, and those charges change. [[loose]]The shape loosens, and the protein stops working. [[range]]So cells keep their inside near pH seven, where one unit of change already means ten times more or less H plus. [[next]]How do they hold it steady? With buffers, in the next lesson.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Water splits rarely, into H plus and hydroxide, ten to the minus seven molar each in pure water. [[w2]]Acids donate protons and raise H plus. Bases accept them and lower it. [[w3]]pH is minus log of H plus. Each step is a factor of ten, and below seven is acidic. [[w4]]Cells stay near seven because protein shape depends on it. [[end]]Now try the practice.
beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of chapter three, lesson four.
